title: A Catholic Educator's Evaluation
author: Liz Cipriano
summary: Liz Cipriano, a Catholic classical educator, evaluates the Front Royal Statement, a set of seven cardinal principles for Catholic K-12 education issued by 45 bishops, scholars, and school leaders following Christendom College's 2026 Education Summit. She frames the statement as a founding document comparable to the Declaration of Independence, articulating principles, including the supernatural end of education and the integrity of curriculum, that closely track classical education's vision even without using the word 'classical.' Cipriano grounds the statement's urgency in a steep institutional decline, from nearly 13,000 U.S. Catholic schools serving over five million students in 1960 to roughly 6,000 schools serving under 1.7 million today, and argues the deeper crisis is curricular: most contemporary Catholic schools have quietly adopted state curricula, including Social Emotional Learning and Common Core math, stripped only of content that directly contradicts Church teaching. She traces the root cause to teacher preparation, noting that most Catholic educators are certified through state programs built to deliver public-school curricula rather than to form students within a specifically Catholic intellectual and sacramental tradition. The piece closes by holding up explicitly 'Catholic Classical' schools, aligned with organizations like the Institute for Catholic Liberal Education, as the exception that already embodies the statement's vision, and frames the choice facing the rest of Catholic education in stark terms: join that model, or continue toward closure.
points: Cipriano frames the Front Royal Statement, signed by 45 Catholic bishops, scholars, and school leaders, as a founding document for Catholic education comparable to the Declaration of Independence.

She documents a steep institutional decline (nearly 13,000 U.S. Catholic schools in 1960 versus 6,000 today, enrollment down from over 5 million to under 1.7 million), used to establish why the statement's principles were necessary.
Her sharpest claim is that most contemporary Catholic schools are Catholic in name only, having adopted state curricula wholesale minus content that directly contradicts Church teaching.

She identifies teacher preparation as the deepest structural cause, since most Catholic educators are certified through state programs that train them to deliver public-school curricula rather than to form students sacramentally.

The piece positions explicitly 'Catholic Classical' schools as the rare exception that actually follows the Front Royal Statement's vision, framing the choice facing Catholic education as existential: 'join, or die.'
quotes: The Front Royal Statement is for Catholic education what the Declaration of Independence was to the American revolutionary colonists: an outline of the basic principles and grievances on which their new nation was born.
The seven principles establish a rich vision of education that classical educators resonate with. And they do so without using the language of "classical.

One of the loveliest lines in the Front Royal Statement reiterates that education is a "restauratio" that heals "the wounds of sin to reorder the soul in an ascent from dispersion to unity. True education forms desire by training a person to recognize, love, and pursue what is truly good, both at the natural and supernatural levels.

In 1874 there were nearly 1,400 Catholic schools in the United States. By 1960 there were almost 13,000 Catholic schools in America, educating over five million students. In 2026, there are only 6,000 Catholic schools in the United States, with an enrollment of under 1.7 million children.

The majority of Catholic schools in the country have adopted the state curriculum, minus the content overtly contrary to the Catholic Church's teachings. On the menu at your run-of-the-mill Catholic school in the United States is: Social Emotional Learning, Common core math curricula (complete with practice on a tablet), no cursive.

The most important change over the past 60 years in Catholic education lies in teacher preparation. Most Catholic educators receive certification or licensure from state run schools training teachers to teach a public school curriculum.

Catholics that want their children to learn from the richness of the beauty of the western theological, intellectual, and philosophical heritage have not been able to trust their children to the local Catholic school down the street, unless that school has specifically made a decision to become a Catholic Classical Liberal Arts school.
